title: To Understand France’s Unrest, Look Back to 1982
gist: French argues that France's student-led protests since late September reflect the dissolution of the postwar conditions underpinning its social model, and that Mitterrand's 1982 forced U-turn under market and currency pressure shows the limits France faces today, now with 119% debt-to-GDP and no national currency. Neither the left's call for state generosity nor Le Pen's anti-immigration, anti-EU program offers a workable answer.

insights.claim: After raising wages, lowering the retirement age, shortening the workweek and nationalizing banks and major industrials in 1981, Mitterrand reversed course in July 1982 with spending cuts, tax hikes, price freezes and a return to inflation control.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Historical precedent for bond and currency markets forcing a French policy reversal.
insights.quote: In July 1982, Mitterrand ordered a cut in public spending, raised taxes, froze prices, and restored the finance ministry’s traditional role of controlling inflation

insights.claim: Mitterrand's program was stopped by the threat of financial markets, the prospect of wealthy people emigrating to avoid taxes, and pressure on the French franc, showing France could not break alone from the capitalist world.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Market discipline constrains expansive fiscal programs in mid-sized open economies.
insights.quote: Mitterrand was stopped in his tracks decades ago by the threat of financial markets, by the prospect that the wealthy would flee taxation by emigrating, and by pressure on the French franc.

insights.claim: France's public debt recently rose to 119 percent of GDP, the third-highest ratio in the European Union.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: High debt limits France's capacity to respond to protest demands with spending, a risk for OAT spreads.
insights.quote: France’s public debt recently rose to 119 percent of GDP, the third-highest ratio in the European Union.

insights.claim: France today has even less room than Mitterrand did because it no longer controls its own currency and its fiscal options are limited by EU policies.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Without devaluation as a release valve, adjustment pressure falls on fiscal policy and social stability.

insights.claim: Emmanuel Macron, deeply unpopular and nearing the end of his final term, has focused on holding the line on a dwindling welfare state while preserving France's great-power self-image.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: An approaching leadership transition adds political uncertainty to French fiscal policy.

insights.claim: Since late September, France has seen some of its largest protests in recent memory, led by high school students over underinvestment in education and growing educational inequality, later joined by citizens disenchanted with the country's failure to deliver prosperity and social benefits.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Broadening social unrest raises French political risk and pressure for unfunded spending.

insights.claim: Europe's postwar prosperity rested on ties to a booming US and favorable demographics from a fertility rebound and high immigration, conditions that no longer exist as the US enters slow growth and Western birth rates fall.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Structural headwinds to European growth and social-security financing are long-lived.
insights.quote: The postwar compact that underwrote European prosperity rested on conditions that no longer exist.

insights.claim: Europe's sense of declining prospects has paradoxically fueled anti-immigrant politics, preventing the replenishment of taxpayer rolls that integrating young immigrants would provide.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Restrictive immigration worsens the fiscal math of aging European welfare states.
insights.locator: All of this has now changed

insights.claim: China, unable to counter its decelerating growth except through ever-larger trade surpluses, threatens the survival of industry in Europe and elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Chinese export overcapacity is a persistent margin threat to European manufacturers.

insights.claim: Europe is squeezed simultaneously by a slower-growing and nearly hostile US under Trump, Chinese trade surpluses, and a Russia waging war in Ukraine and threatening NATO borderland countries.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: A three-front external squeeze weighs on European growth and raises defense spending needs.

insights.claim: Marine Le Pen's leading opposition party promises revival through sharply reduced immigration, austerity and a much-weakened EU, which the author considers even more unworkable than the left's call for state generosity.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: A Le Pen victory with an EU-weakening agenda would be a significant risk for French bonds and euro cohesion.

insights.claim: France's real crisis is not the choice of leaders but that the conditions making its social model attractive have dissolved, and no political movement on the left or right has honestly reckoned with that.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Expect continued political instability and policy drift regardless of who governs.
insights.quote: the conditions that made its social model attractive have dissolved, and no political movement left or right has yet to reckon honestly with that fact.

insights.claim: France's lessons apply to a growing number of Western countries, including Britain and Germany, whose economies are wracked by crisis and whose politics are swept up in populism.
insights.speaker: Howard W. French
insights.so_what: Fiscal-social stress and populism are a pan-Western, not uniquely French, risk factor.
